variable-meaning.why: A letter in algebra stands for a number you do not yet know, or one that can vary. That is a smaller idea than it looks, and it is the hinge the whole subject turns on: once quantities have names, you can state relationships before you know the values.
traps: A letter is not a label for an object. In ~5a~, if ~a~ is the price of an apple then ~5a~ is a cost, not five apples.

code.body:
price = 3        # a variable in code HOLDS a value
total = 5 * price

# in algebra, 5p = 15 means p is UNKNOWN; you solve for it
code.note: Same word, two different meanings. In code a variable is a labelled box you put values in; in algebra it is an unknown you deduce. Keeping them apart saves a lot of confusion later.

translate-expressions.why: Most algebra mistakes are translation mistakes made before any algebra started. English puts things in an order that symbols sometimes reverse, and a handful of phrases are reliably treacherous.
traps: '5 less than x' is ~x - 5~, not ~5 - x~. 'x subtracted from 5' is ~5 - x~. Read these aloud slowly, every time.

evaluate-expressions.why: Evaluating is substitution followed by the order of operations. Putting brackets round every substituted value, especially negatives, removes most of the risk: ~x^{2}~ at ~x = -3~ is ~(-3)^{2} = 9~.
traps: Substitute into *every* occurrence of the letter, not just the first.

terms-coefficients.why: Terms are separated by + and - at the top level; the coefficient is the number multiplying a term, carrying its own sign. Naming the parts precisely is what lets you follow instructions like 'collect like terms' without guessing.
traps: The sign belongs to the coefficient. In ~3x - 7y~ the coefficient of ~y~ is -7, not 7.
